content: 1. Position the woman with her buttocks at the edge of the bed or in an all-fours position (on hands and knees). 2. Avoid performing episiotomy routinely. 3. Allow the buttocks, trunk, and shoulders of the baby to deliver spontaneously during contractions. 4. After the shoulders are delivered, let the baby hang until the next contraction. 5. If the head does not deliver after several contractions, place the baby astride your left forearm with its limbs hanging on either side. 6. Use the middle and index fingers of your left hand to apply gentle downward pressure on the malar cheekbones to aid in flexing the baby’s head. 7. While maintaining the left hand’s position, use the index and ring fingers of your right hand to support the baby’s shoulders and the middle finger to gently flex the baby’s head until the hairline becomes visible. 8. Once the hairline is visible, lift the baby upward and forward toward the mother’s abdomen until the nose and mouth are free. 9. During this process, an assistant should apply suprapubic pressure to maintain head flexion. 10. If the baby’s arms or shoulders are trapped, feel the baby’s chest for the arms. If the arms are not felt, gently hold the baby by placing your hands around each thigh with your thumbs on the sacrum. 11. Guide the baby downward and rotate it, keeping the back uppermost, until the posterior shoulder becomes anterior and the arm is released. 12. Rotate the baby back, keeping the back uppermost, to deliver the other arm. 13. Proceed with the delivery of the head as previously described. 14. If the head is trapped and the baby is deceased, proceed with the delivery of the head as described above. 15. Never pull on the breech. 16. Do not allow the woman to push until the cervix is fully dilated, as premature pushing may trap the head. 17. Call for additional help and prepare for newborn resuscitation. 18. Explain the situation to the woman and her companion. 19. Ask the woman to lie on her back, flex her legs tightly against her chest, and keep her knees wide apart. Have a companion or assistant maintain this position. 20. Avoid routine episiotomy. 21. Ask an assistant to apply continuous downward pressure on the abdomen above the pubic area while you maintain downward traction on the fetal head. 22. Stay calm and explain to the woman that her cooperation is needed to try another position. 23. Assist her into an all-fours position and have her companion stabilize her. This position change may sometimes dislodge an impacted shoulder and facilitate delivery. 24. If necessary, introduce your right hand into the vagina along the posterior curve of the sacrum. 25. Attempt to deliver the posterior shoulder or arm by hooking it downward and forward through the vagina using your fingers. 26. Complete the rest of the delivery as normal. 27. If unsuccessful, urgently refer the woman to a hospital. Avoid excessive pulling on the head. For multiple births: 28. Prepare the delivery room and equipment for the birth of two or more babies, including warm cloths, two sets of cord ties and blades, and resuscitation equipment for two babies. 29. Arrange for a helper to assist with the births and care of the babies. 30. Deliver the first baby following standard procedures, resuscitating if necessary, and label the baby as Twin 1. 31. Have the helper attend to the first baby. 32. Palpate the uterus immediately to determine the position of the second baby. If the baby is in a transverse or oblique lie, gently turn it to a head or breech presentation using abdominal manipulation. 33. Confirm the presentation with a vaginal examination and check the fetal heart rate. 34. Wait for strong contractions to return and for the second bag of membranes to rupture, which usually occurs within one hour of the first baby’s birth but may take longer. 35. Stay with the woman and monitor her and the fetal heart rate closely. 36. Remove wet cloths from underneath her and cover her if she feels chilled. 37. When the membranes rupture, perform a vaginal examination to check for a prolapsed cord. If present, manage accordingly. 38. When strong contractions resume, ask the mother to bear down when she feels ready. 39. Deliver the second baby, resuscitating if necessary, and label the baby as Twin 2. 40. After cutting the cord, have the helper attend to the second baby. 41. Palpate the uterus for a third baby. If present, proceed as described above. If no third baby is felt, move to the third stage of labor. 42. Do not attempt to deliver the placenta until all babies are born. 43. Do not administer oxytocin until after the birth of all babies. Third stage of labor: 44. Administer 10 IU of oxytocin intramuscularly after confirming no additional babies are present. 45. Once the uterus is well-contracted, deliver the placenta and membranes by applying traction to all cords together. 46. Observe closely for vaginal bleeding before and after placenta delivery, as the woman is at higher risk of postpartum hemorrhage. 47. If the placenta is incomplete, manage accordingly. 48. Examine the placenta and membranes for completeness. There may be one large placenta with two umbilical cords or separate placentas for each baby. Immediate postpartum care: 49. Monitor the woman and newborn intensively, as the risk of bleeding is increased. 50. Keep the mother and baby in the health facility for at least 24 hours after birth. 51. Plan to measure postpartum hemoglobin if possible. 52. Provide special support for the care and feeding of the babies. 53. Keep the mother and baby together in the delivery room and do not separate them. 54. Never leave the woman and newborn alone. 55. Encourage the woman to eat, drink, and rest. 56. Ensure the mother has sanitary napkins or clean material to collect vaginal blood. 57. Advise on postpartum care, hygiene, and nutrition. 58. Counsel on family planning and healthy timing and spacing of pregnancies. 59. Reassess the mother and baby before discharge. 60. If the mother desires tubal ligation, refer her to a hospital within seven days of delivery. If she desires an IUD, refer her to appropriate services within 48 hours. For complications: 61. If heavy vaginal bleeding occurs, palpate the uterus. If it is not firm, massage the fundus to encourage contraction and expel clots. 62. If the bleeding is from a perineal tear, repair it or refer to a hospital. 63. If the mother cannot pass urine or the bladder is full, assist her by gently pouring water on the vulva. Avoid catheterization unless absolutely necessary. 64. If fever persists, monitor temperature every four hours and administer antibiotics if necessary. Refer to a hospital if the fever continues for more than 12 hours or rises rapidly. 65. For severe anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL), refer the woman urgently to a hospital. For moderate anemia (hemoglobin 7–11 g/dL), provide a double dose of iron for three months and recheck hemoglobin after three days. 66. If diastolic blood pressure is ≥90 mmHg, monitor closely and refer to a hospital if pre-eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia is suspected.
